https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/uk-settlement-.text: The number of migrants granted permanent settlement in the UK has reached its highest level since 2010, Home Office figures show, as almost 200,000 people secured their status in the year to June ahead of planned tightening of residency rules.Settlement grants, formally known as indefinite leave to remain, rose to 199,628 in the year ending June 2026, up 24 per cent on the previous year.The rise comes ahead of proposed reforms that would double the qualifying period for settlement from five years to 10, a change announced by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood but initially put forward by the previous prime minister.Officials said the increase was driven largely by former work visa holders and a surge in approvals for Hong Kong British National (Overseas) visa holders, whose settlement grants rose from 587 to 38,373 over the year.Settlement Grants at Highest Level in 16 YearsHome Office statisticians also recorded 315,224 citizenship applications over the same period, a record total and a 17 per cent rise on the year before.Applications from EU nationals climbed by around 40 per cent to more than 81,000, a jump researchers at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford said did not match any equivalent rise in the number of EU citizens newly eligible to apply.The proposed changes to indefinite leave to remain were first put forward under Burnham's predecessor as prime minister, Keir Starmer, and remain under government consultation.Andy Burnham, who succeeded Starmer, now faces pressure from within his own party to reconsider whether to press ahead. The plan has divided Labour MPs, some of whom argue it risks leaving long-term residents in prolonged uncertainty.Burnham also faces pressure from the right, with the Conservatives and Reform UK both suggesting they would strip settlement rights from some people who already hold them.Who Is Applying, and Why Numbers Are RisingIndian nationals remained the largest group granted settlement, with 35,384 grants, up 51 per cent, largely reflecting workers who arrived on employment routes some years ago and have now reached the end of their qualifying period.Grants to Chinese nationals almost quadrupled to 21,300. Grants to people with refugee or protection-based status fell by 40 per cent to 22,799, which the Home Office linked to fewer protection decisions made during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.Nuni Jorgensen, a researcher at the Migration Observatory, said the pattern pointed to something beyond routine administrative timing.'The higher number of people applying for citizenship partly reflects rising non-EU migration even before Brexit, as well as a gradual increase in the share of non-EU migrants choosing to become citizens since 2021,' she said.'Among EU citizens, the increase is particularly sharp and suggests a more sudden change in people's desire to become British.'She stopped short of drawing a firm line between the policy debate and the applications themselves. 'The data do not tell us why, although it is possible that government and opposition party debates about restricting rights or removing people without citizenship may have played a role.Research suggests that uncertainty can encourage migrants to secure their status by applying for citizenship,' she said. More than 9,400 Americans applied for British citizenship over the year, though the US remained well behind India, Pakistan, Italy, Nigeria, Romania and Poland in the overall rankings.Asylum Changes May Shape Future Settlement NumbersSeparately, the number of asylum seekers housed in hotels fell by half over the year to 16,021 by the end of June, the lowest total since the Home Office began publishing the figure in 2022. Mahmood said the government was 'restoring control' of the asylum system.According to the Migration Observatory, the fall was chiefly due to a shrinking initial decision backlog rather than any resolution in the separate appeals system, where a backlog has continued to grow. That distinction may end up mattering more to next year's settlement figures than anything decided in the current consultation.

https://original.antiwar.com/richard_eda.text: How Britain Tried To Rig the Trial of a Genocide Opponent – and Lost by Richard Edain | Sep 7, 2026 | 0 comments The jury took just two hours. Tony Greenstein – Jewish socialist, anti-Zionist – had faced fourteen years under the Terrorism Act for three social media posts and a blog article opposing Israel’s genocide in Gaza. The Crown called it “inviting support for Hamas.” The jury called it something else. Section 12 of the Terrorism Act makes it an offense to invite support for a proscribed organization. Greenstein’s reference to a “Gaza ghetto uprising”, it argued, amounted to support for Hamas. Three social media posts and a blog article. The bill the State was demanding for those words – fourteen years. Judge Sarah Plaschkes repeatedly objected when Greenstein brought the wider historical-political context of Palestine/Israel into the courtroom – warning him against treating the proceedings as a political forum. When the closing speech came, Greenstein was by now so concerned about what might happen to his barrister that he decided to address the jury himself (no doubt considering what had happened to Barrister Rajiv Menon KC – more of whom later). For thirty minutes he examined the prosecution case and the context in which his posts had been written. The jury wasn’t asked to lay aside the offending words; instead, he guided the jurors in an articulate reading ( see his address to the jury, here ) in which the world in which they’d been written was made clear ( full trial coverage at the Canary, here ). But this court was rigged and thus determined to keep all context out of the courtroom. Nevertheless, despite Judge Plaschkes’ hostile interruptions, Greenstein’s speech laid bare the realities the prosecution had no interest in facing: his opposition to Hamas evident in dozens of articles he’d penned and published on his platform over the years; and Israel’s genocide in Gaza after October 2023. He spelled out the difference between supporting Hamas and defending the right of Palestinians to resist Israeli oppression, and the obvious point that the posts in contention clearly did not express support for Hamas. Greenstein recounted to the jury how his grandparents fled Poland before the War, and most of those left behind perished in Treblinka. To him, Greenstein told the jury, the Holocaust was not history, but inheritance. He invoked the story of the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto uprising as a parallel of Gaza: young Jewish men and women rising up against the SS with smuggled pistols against tanks, knowing it was hopeless yet choosing resistance anyway. October 7th was Gaza’s uprising. The judge objected. Once Greenstein had finished speaking (to a round of applause from the public gallery), Judge Plaschkes addressed the court to say that she had considered referring Greenstein for contempt of court. She then dismissed his address as a “rambling speech delivered by an old man” . An extraordinary turn of phrase in a criminal trial in which Greenstein was about to find out whether he was to be sentenced to 14 years in prison. Home Secretary Yvette Cooper added Palestine Action to the UK’s list of proscribed organizations in July 2025, under section 3 of the Terrorism Act 2000 . But proscription criminalizes more than membership. Up to fourteen years in prison can follow under section 12 , which makes it an offence to “invite support for a proscribed organization” or to “express an opinion or belief that is supportive of a proscribed organization…” That was the provision the Crown used to prosecute Tony Greenstein, and it applies right now to public expressions of support for Palestine Action. Serious concerns over freedom of expression and peaceful assembly were raised by a group of five UN Special Rapporteurs over proscribing a group for property destruction. On 6 August 2024 activists from Palestine Action staged a break-in at Elbit Systems , in Filton, near Bristol. It’s an Israeli defense company with British operations supplying equipment to the IDF. They entered facilities, sabotaged machinery and hindered production they regarded as part of Israel’s war-making infrastructure. During the parliamentary debate on the proscription order, it was argued that Palestine Action had targeted only industrial facilities, and not civilians . The government went ahead with proscription anyway. Rajiv Menon KC represented one of the six defendants in the February 2026 Filton Trial. All six were acquitted of aggravated burglary but the jury failed to agree on criminal damage. At the May retrial, four were convicted . Menon’s closing speech was a masterclass and invoked the 1670 Bushell case – a landmark ruling on jury independence from judicial interference, arguing that the judge could not direct a conviction. Judge Jeremy Johnson then referred Menon for contempt, a referral the Court of Appeal overturned on procedural grounds in May b efore Johnson referred to it correctly in June. The Filton defendants were acquitted of the most serious charge – t he barrister who defended them is now facing contempt proceedings for the way he did it . So what lies behind all this courtroom drama is a routine machinery. Proscription – the government’s designation of an organization as terrorist – takes effect by order of the Home Secretary. It falls to the barrister to gauge how far a closing speech can go before crossing the line into contempt, while the judge cautions against political argument. Indeed, the evidence shows that judges are increasingly directing what juries are allowed to hear before threatening barristers with contempt. To an outside observer there is little sign of a conflict – yet behind these routine procedures is something damning: what the jury doesn’t get to hear – could mean years in prison. And, of course, the elephant in the room is that Britain is directly implicated in Israel’s genocide in Gaza. In September 2024, as the government suspended thirty arms export licenses to Israel, Foreign Secretary David Lammy told Parliament that “there exists a clear risk that they might be used to commit or facilitate a serious violation of international humanitarian law” . Thirty licenses suspended out of three hundred and fifty. Britain would also continue to supply F-35 components through the global parts pool serving Israel, with the government arguing that withdrawal would undermine allied security. British weapons armed a state committing a genocide despite their supposed withdrawal. The state that arms Israel prosecutes those who oppose it. The Crown had brought three posts, a blog article and an accusation of terrorism before the jury. But Greenstein stood on that essential context – despite the hostile judge’s interjections. And a mere two hours after retiring – the jurors returned with a unanimous verdict of not guilty. Richard Edain is a teacher and writer based in the UK and Vietnam. Opposed to imperialism, his work focuses on tracing today’s global headlines back to their historical roots. His work appears on Substack as the Ulysses Files . https://hotair.com/mitch_berg/2026/09/27.text: Rumor of War Mitch Berg 10:00 AM | September 27, 2026 AP Photo/Sergei Stepanov While the world focuses on the Straits of Hormuz and the blood-sodden fields of Zaporizhye, and conventional political wonks looked for tea leaves in Russia's fake election, people who follow Eastern European shenanigans are looking nervously at the border between Estonia and Russia. Stephen Green notes that the si gns along the Narva River are getting ominous : Russia's internal security service has announced a curfew and restrictions along part of its border with NATO member Estonia. Civilians have been banned from leaving villages after dark, boating on the Narva River, and hunting within 5km of the border. pic.twitter.com/iInuthxsIG — OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) September 20, 2026 "There are intelligence reports that Russia has been building hospital facilities" on the Estonia border, while "Russian border guards have been spotted shoring up the banks of the Narva River in exactly the way you would expect if you thought they were going to throw expedient military bridges across it." "Russian border guards have also removed a set of buoys in the river marking the Russian-Estonian border, sparking a formal protest from the Estonian government," Eric added, literally muddying the waters between the two countries. But here's where it gets truly disturbing: "The city of Narva, Estonia, sits at the Russian border, on the Narva river, opposite the zone where the Russians have declared a curfew for its inhabitants and a no-go zone for people who don't already live there." Estonia has a sizeable Russian minority — and if you think this bit of history rhymes with "Sudetenland", you're thinking what I'm thinking. I was about to write "one huge difference between Estonia today and Czechoslovakia in 1938 is that Estonia is a NATO member"... https://pjmedia.com/vodkapundit/2026/09/21/who-had-world-war-iii-starting-in-estonia-on-their-2026-bingo-card-n4957473 Russia's internal security service has announced a curfew and restrictions along part of its border with NATO member Estonia. Civilians have been banned from leaving villages after dark, boating on the Narva River, and hunting within 5km of the border. pic.twitter.com/iInuthxsIG — OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) September 20, 2026 ...until I remembered that the Czechs had powerful allies on France and Britain. Neville Chamberlain proclaims "peace in our time" after allowing Nazi Germany to annex Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland, September 30, 1938. pic.twitter.com/iSGNo8g0FO — Historic Vids (@historyinmemes) October 30, 2025 Will Europe - backed by the United States, of course — do better this time around? Europeans — unbeknownst to most Americans — are certainly paying attention: I can understand why countries like Poland, Estonia, Finland or Sweden are so worried about Russia (geographical proximity, troubled shared history, etc.) but Spain and Portugal are a surprise to me: pic.twitter.com/GjUgFJCqvn — Wojciech Pawelczyk (@WojPawelczyk) September 8, 2026 So, history aside, how will NATO fare against an attack that appears intended to try to fracture NATO? Intelligence mavens "joke", laughing grimly, that Poland would love nothing more than to attack Russia. I once heard a joke — or "joke" - that someone once asked a Polish soldier that if Germany and Russia invaded Poland again, who would he shoot first? He responded "The German. Business before pleasure". They have hundreds of years of unfinished business with the Russians. Speaking of unfinished business, Estonia has been soberly eyeing its carnivorous neighbor for its entire free existence. This article from 2018 is a long, fascinating, deeply sobering read about a tiny country (a little over a million people) which has made the idea of fighting a guerrilla war against Russians a national pastime. The moderately alert among you may ask "But wait - haven't the Russians been bled white in Ukraine?" They have. Depending on the reports you believe, they may actually be running out of their once-massive stockpiles of tanks, personnel carriers, artillery, and volunteers. But as Green notes: But then I'm reminded of a quote attributed to Dwight Eisenhower: "If a problem cannot be solved, enlarge it." Russia's recent "elections" have been seen as providing Putin political cover to order a "mobilization" - to start mass conscription to beef up the Army. Those who've observed Ukraine might point out that throwing uniforms on civilians with a few weeks military training and throwing them into the front lines — which is what they've been doing in Ukraine recently — results in stacks of dead bodies, roads full of maimed young men, and roads full of charred tanks. And there's no reason to believe an attack against NATO — especially an Estonia that's got thousands of reservists hiding in the dense Estonian forests and a Polish army that is licking its chops and eager to avenge 1939, Katyn Wood, the betrayal of the Warsaw Uprising and four decades of Communism — will go much better. But the one part of the Russian military that isn't nearly comatose from blood loss are their "Strategic Rocket Forces" - the nukes. Forget about Estonians hunting down conscripts in the forest, or Polish "winged Hussars" in Leopard 2s sacking Smolensk. The question after the first round of conscripts gets mowed down will be "are you, NATO, willing to risk losing Warsaw to protect Talinn? Yes? How about Bremen, Lyon or Birmingham? Cleveland?" Our media isn't likely to cover this until it's far too late. In short: Belgium's Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot says Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinian civilians, European diplomats and a French mayor in the occupied West Bank. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar described the perpetrators as Israeli rioters. Palestinian Vice-President Hussein al-Sheikh called the attack a small example of the "daily terrorism" to which Palestinians are subjected. abc.net.au/news/israeli-settler-attack-palestinians-european-diplomats-west-bank/107280242 Link copied Share Share article Masked settlers have attacked a group of European diplomats during a visit to the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Belgium's foreign minister says. Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian civilians, French and Polish diplomats, Belgium's consul general to the Palestinians and a French mayor, Maxime Prevot said. The attacks came a day after settlers beat an American photojournalist . A video still of the site where Belgium's foreign minister says masked settlers attacked Palestinians, Catholic representatives and Western diplomats and officials. ( Reuters: Emad Diab ) "As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. Impunity for violent settlers must end," Mr Prevot said in a statement posted on X. A Belgian vehicle was also damaged, he said. 'Thrown to the ground' Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, told Reuters he had been harvesting olives near the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh in solidarity with the local community when he was "violently attacked" by masked settlers. "I was thrown to the ground," he said. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the attack, describing the perpetrators as Israeli rioters. He also suggested the diplomats should have coordinated their visit with the Israeli military. 'Israeli terrorists' target villagers' homes in days-long siege Palestinians in a small West Bank village have spent almost a week under siege from Israeli settlers, with members of the community accusing the Israeli military of complicity in the saga. "Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security," he said in a statement on X. Palestinian Vice-President Hussein al-Sheikh condemned the attack, calling it a small example of the "daily terrorism" to which Palestinians are subjected. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office later issued a statement warning against "premature conclusions" in the incident and noted concerns about "a coordinated campaign to smear Israel". Israeli officials, including Mr Netanyahu, have periodically condemned settler violence, while saying it is carried out by a small minority. Palestinians and human rights groups dispute that characterisation. Israeli police open investigation Settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank have surged over the past three years. Journalists, activists and foreign observers have also been targeted. Firefighters douse a burnt car with water after Israeli settlers attacked a group of Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank. ( Reuters: Ammar Awad ) On Friday, dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank. Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a US citizen covering the harvest, was hospitalised after being assaulted by masked settlers. "Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," Mr Prevot said. Belgium, which has announced a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and the Golan Heights, will press for European Union sanctions "against those responsible for this violence and those who support them", he said. Loading... Polish Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maciej Wewior said on X that a convoy carrying diplomats, including Polish officials, had been attacked. The Polish diplomats were unharmed. "Attacks on members of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable," he said. Israeli police said they had opened an investigation into the incident. There was no immediate announcement of any arrests. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States wanted Israel to do more to ​deter attacks committed by settlers. "We're very disturbed ​by those ‌images and what we're seeing," Mr Rubio said. "We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crackdown on that ‌stuff." Prosecutions of settlers accused of violent crimes against Palestinians in the West Bank are rare. The UN and much of the international community consider the settlements, many of them resembling developed suburbs, in the West Bank to be illegally occupied. Settlers have established hundreds of additional outposts without government authorisation, while still enjoying protection from the Israeli military.
